transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-12-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendoza (Head of Cloud, Sable Harbor), Priya Singh (Security Architect), Evan Brooks (SRE), Asha Iyer (Product)

Summary: quick run through of Sable Harbor's networking constraints and security needs for a Private deployment. Focus on how Redwood would attach into their VPCs, options for private control plane, and region restrictions for EU-resident datasets.

00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh I'm Jordan, I'll be your AE. Quick roll call?
00:08 Carlos Mendoza: Hey Jordan, Carlos here. Head of Cloud at Sable Harbor.
00:11 Priya Singh: Priya here, security.
:13 Evan Brooks: Evan, SRE.
00:15 Jordan: Great. Maya from our infra team is on to go deep on the network. Maya?
00:20 Maya Patel: Hi all. I'll focus on the VPC connectivity patterns and what we need to make private deployment run smoothly, e.g. peering, private endpoints, and how the control plane sits.
00:30 Carlos: Cool. To set context, we're evaluating three options: hosted for dev, dedicated for prod if pricing works, and private in our account for regulated clients. The main blockers are residency and no public egress for production models.
00:45 Jordan: Makes sense. Priya, any immediate security constraints?
00:48 Priya: SOC 2 baseline plus we need KMS integration with our HSM — no key material leaves our environment. Also audit logs need to ship to our SIEM, and SSO via SAML.
01:02 Maya: OK, good. On KMS we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations in Private mode — typical pattern is bring-your-own-key for the model encryption at rest and control plane secrets. We'll send the exact KMS stub later.
01:18 Evan: How's the control plane hosted in Private? Is there a public-facing control plane or will it be in our VPC?
01:25 Jordan: Two flavors — private with customer-managed control plane (control plane endpoints in your VPC) or private with a thin public control plane that uses private endpoints. For full air-gap on-prem we can do an on-prem bundle. For cloud VPCs we generally offer Private Endpoints (PrivateLink/Endpoint Service) or VPC peering depending on provider.
01:45 Priya: We prefer no public endpoints. PrivateLink is better than peering for cross-account IAM boundaries, right? We heard peering distributes route tables and can be messy with overlapping CIDR.
01:58 Maya: Yes, PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink) is usually safer cross-account. It avoids pushing routes into your tables, and it's easier for egress control. However, PrivateLink has per-AZ ENI and cross-region support considerations. For large throughput workloads peering + Transit Gateway can be more cost effective if you control both accounts.
02:18 Carlos: We have multiple AWS accounts across business units; central networking team uses Transit Gateway for east-west. Would Redwood attach to our TGW or do you prefer direct peering?
02:29 Maya: We can integrate with Transit Gateway; many customers attach via TGW to keep topology centralized. Important items: need to know your TGW route propagation, whether you're using AWS Network Firewall, and any NAT egress policy. We'll need the TGW ARN and the attachment workflow.
02:44 Evan: Also need to confirm CIDR space. We have RFC1918 ranges but some older accounts have overlaps. What's Redwood's CIDR requirement?
02:53 Maya: For PrivateLink we don't require a specific CIDR on your side; for peering/ENI we ask for a /28 for control plane endpoints and a few /24s for serving subnets depending on capacity. We'll provide exact recommendations in the topology doc.
03:10 Priya: EU data residency — some of our customers in EU require model execution and logs to remain in eu-central-1. Does Redwood spin up region-local serving?
03:20 Jordan: Yes, we can pin model variants and serving pools to regions. We run region-local clusters; the important bit is whether the control plane can be central or also needs to be region-local. We support region-local control planes in Private.
03:36 Priya: If control plane is region-local, how do we handle SSO and audit aggregation?
03:42 Maya: SSO via SAML/OIDC can federate across regions; audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM using remote logging endpoints or via a log-forwarder inside your VPC. We'll need to confirm log retention and encryption-in-transit expectations.
04:02 Carlos: On egress, we can't have traffic to public internet. Any model checkpoints or container images that Redwood needs — how are those pulled?
04:12 Maya: Two options: we can allow image pulls via a customer-controlled NAT/egress with a whitelist for Redwood artifact repos, or we can pre-stage images into an ECR in your account through a secure pipeline. Many customers prefer pre-staged image flow for compliance.
04:28 Asha Iyer: Ok from product side — pilot success criteria: <100ms 1-p99 latency for short prompt paths, and end-to-end SLA for throughput. Can Redwood run perf tests in our environment?
04:45 Maya: Yes, we can run a benchmark agent inside your VPC — we'll need a small test instance and some synthetic traffic. We'll coordinate scope in the workshop.
04:53 Evan: How about TLS and mTLS for inter-service traffic?
04:58 Maya: We support mTLS and can require client certs for internal endpoints. For PrivateLink-based control plane we can also negotiate mutual TLS.
05:10 Priya: Anything about DNS? We run split-horizon DNS and don't want Redwood to force external names into our resolver.
05:18 Maya: We recommend using private hosted zones and conditional forwarding. For PrivateLink we provide DNS entries that can be imported into your private zone; for peering you may need to add records in your internal DNS. We'll produce a DNS operations checklist.
05:35 Jordan: Quick note on pricing: Private deployments and dedicated capacity have both fixed monthly commit and usage components — I'll share an initial estimate after we scope capacity.
05:46 Carlos: What about failure modes — if a region goes down do you have fallback to another region, and what's the data residency impact?
05:56 Maya: We support automatic failover for availability but not for data residency constrained workloads — if a customer requires strict EU-only execution we will not failover to non-EU without explicit approval. We can configure multi-region active-active within EU regions.
06:12 Priya: Good. On audit/logging — can we get a sample schema for Redwood logs so we can confirm SIEM ingestion?
06:20 Jordan: Absolutely — action item for Maya to dump the log schema and an example JSON.
06:26 (crosstalk) Evan: One more question about routes — we use some VPC endpoints already; will Redwood require route table propagation changes?
06:33 Maya: For Transit Gateway attachments you'll likely need route propagation; we try to limit changes to a single route table we agree on. For PrivateLink almost no route table changes are needed, just ENI provisioning in your subnets.
06:48 Priya: Any compliance evidence we can review before legal signs off? We need SOC 2 Type II, ISO27001, pentest reports, etc.
06:56 Jordan: We have SOC 2 and ISO certs — I'll drop those and a security whitepaper. For pentests we'll share redacted summary findings and our vulnerability management process.
07:07 Carlos: Great. How about onboarding timeline? If we sign, can we pilot in Q1 2027?
07:14 Jordan: Yes, Q1 pilot is reasonable. Workshop first week of Dec to lock topology, then pilot prepped in Jan.
07:22 Maya: For the workshop, we'll need network engineers and your TGW admins. We'll run a 90-min session, collect CIDRs, subnets, and IAM patterns.
07:31 Priya: We also need a data flow diagram to show where logs and telemetry go.
07:36 Jordan: We'll include that in the topo doc.
07:39 (long pause, note taking)
07:45 Evan: One implementation detail — how is KV cache handled? We want to ensure no PII is cached unless encrypted.
07:53 Maya: We can disable KV caching for sensitive models; otherwise KV caches live on the serving plane and are encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys if configured. We'll include caching options in the pilot config.
08:10 Carlos: Anything else? I heard mention of burst capacity — we need occasional spikes for end-of-quarter.
08:17 Jordan: We support burst capacity on Dedicated and Private with a negotiated buffer. We'll outline burst terms in the pricing doc.
08:26 Asha: For the pilot, success metrics again: latency, cost per 1k tokens, and security checklist complete.
08:33 Jordan: Yup. We'll align on exact thresholds in the pilot scope doc.
08:38 (wrap-up) Jordan: To recap next steps: schedule the network workshop, Jordan to send pricing and compliance docs, Maya to send CIDR and DNS checklist + log schema, Sable Harbor to share TGW info and current network diagram.
08:55 Priya: Sounds good. One final ask — please obfuscate any internal hostnames in docs before sending.
09:02 Jordan: Will do. Thanks everyone, talk soon.

Action items (in transcript):
- Jordan: Send SOC2/ISO docs, pricing sheet, and topology template.
- Maya: Send CIDR recommendations, DNS ops checklist, log schema, and benchmark agent requirements.
- Sable Harbor (Priya/Carlos): Provide TGW ARN, current VPC diagrams, and list of sensitive datasets that must not leave EU.

Links referenced: "Private deployment topology template" (link to be shared), security whitepaper (link), pricing spreadsheet (link).

End of transcript.
